chapters.title: Chapter 2: Intangible Assets: Brands, Patents, and Licences

lessons.title: When a Famous Brand Is Not a Moat

body.text: Everyone in India knew the name Onida. Everyone knew HMT. Fame did not save either of them. Awareness is not a moat. Pricing power is.

children.text: The last lesson showed how a brand creates a moat through pricing power. This lesson covers the far more common case: a brand everyone recognises that gives the company almost no protection. Learning to spot these saves investors from paying moat valuations for businesses that do not have one.
Famous Names That Could Not Hold Their Ground

body.caption: Iconic Indian brands and why their fame was not a moat

body.text: Look closely at Kingfisher. United Breweries' Kingfisher beer has long been a dominant brand. The same name, the same promoter group, and the same marketing flair produced a failed airline. The brand was never the moat. The economics of the industry decided the outcome.

body.title: Two very different things that both get called "a strong brand"

columns.label: Brand awareness
points: Customers recognise the name and logo
Any well-funded rival can buy the same awareness
Customers still compare prices before buying
Shows up in surveys and social media followers

columns.label: Brand-based pricing power
points: Customers pay more and keep buying
Built over years of trust, habit, or professional loyalty
Customers do not seriously consider alternatives
Shows up in stable gross margins and high ROCE

children.text: Five Situations Where a Brand Fails to Protect Profits
1. The Customer Buys on Specification or Price

Airline seats, telecom data, televisions, and most commodity-like products are compared on a screen before purchase. When a customer can line up alternatives side by side, the brand becomes a tiebreaker, not a reason to pay more.
2. Technology Changes What the Customer Needs

HMT made good mechanical watches. When the market shifted to quartz and then to design-led fashion watches, its brand stood for the wrong product. A brand protects a company only as long as customers still want what it stands for.
3. The Brand Is Stretched into a Different Industry

A name that means quality in one category often means nothing in another. Brand extensions work when the trust genuinely transfers, such as a paint company moving into waterproofing. They fail when the new industry has its own harsher economics, as Kingfisher found in aviation.

markDefs.definition: Advertising and promotion expenses as a percentage of sales. A rising ratio without a matching rise in pricing or share can signal a brand that needs increasing support.

children.text: If a company must keep raising advertising, promotions, and discounts just to hold its market share, the brand is being rented, not owned. Watch
in the annual report over several years.
5. Distribution Shifts Away from the Brand's Strength

Some brands were built on shelf space in traditional kirana stores. As more buying moves to modern trade, e-commerce, and quick commerce apps, retailers' private labels and digital-first brands get direct access to customers. A brand that relied on being the only familiar name on the shelf loses that advantage when shoppers scroll and compare instead.
A hypothetical consumer brand keeps its market share over four years. On the surface, nothing has changed. Here is what happened underneath.

stats.context: Could not fully pass on cost increases

stats.label: A&P as % of sales

body.title: Find the Margin Damage
body.prompt: Using the stat grid above, operating margin = gross margin − A&P − other operating costs. By how many percentage points did the operating margin fall over the four years?
body.explanation: Before: 45% − 8% − 20% = 17%. After: 43% − 12% − 20% = 11%. Operating margin fell by 6 percentage points, more than a third of its original level, while market share looked perfectly stable. A brand with real pricing power would have held gross margin without needing 50% more ad spend relative to sales.

body.title: Illustrative: A Brand Being Rented, Not Owned (% of Sales)
Moat Brand or Famous Name?
body.question: A listed consumer electronics company has one of the most recognised brand names in India. Over five years, its gross margin has fallen from 30% to 22%, it has matched every competitor's festive discount, and its market share has slipped slightly. What is the best description?
options: A moat brand going through a temporary rough patch
A famous name without pricing power, in a category where customers buy on specification and price
A moat business, because brand recognition is high
A company with a network effect moat
body.explanation: Falling gross margins, matching discounts, and slipping share are the opposite of pricing power. Recognition is high, but customers clearly compare on price and specification. That is a famous name, not a moat.

body.title: Warning Signs a Brand Is Not a Moat

cards.definition: The company cannot pass on cost increases, so customers are not paying for the brand.
More spending is needed just to hold the same share. The brand is being rented.
Customers switch on price, so the brand cannot hold a premium.
Buyers compare features and prices side by side, so brand becomes a tiebreaker.

cards.term: Brand stretched into a new industry
cards.definition: Trust built in one category rarely overcomes the economics of another.

body.title: The Celebrity Brand IPO
body.scenario: A consumer company plans an IPO on the NSE. It sells athleisure clothing under a brand co-founded by a famous cricketer. It has 8 million Instagram followers, revenue has grown 60% a year for three years, and the offer document highlights "India's most loved youth brand". A&P spend is 18% of sales, most sales happen during online discount events, and the company has not yet made an operating profit.
body.prompt: Is this brand a moat? What would you need to see before paying a premium valuation?
body.modelAnswer: On current evidence, no. Followers and fame are awareness, not pricing power. Clothing is a category where tastes shift and customers compare options easily, especially online. Heavy reliance on discount events suggests customers buy on price, and 18% A&P with no operating profit means the brand is being bought with spending. Dependence on one celebrity adds key-person risk. Before paying a premium, you would want to see: full-price sales becoming a larger share of revenue; gross margins holding or rising as the company scales; A&P as a percentage of sales falling while growth continues; repeat purchase rates from existing customers; and eventually, ROCE above the cost of capital. Until then, value it as a fast-growing apparel business, not a moat business.

body.title: Stress-Test a Famous Brand
steps: Pick a listed company whose brand everyone knows
Ask whether its customers buy on specification and price or on trust and habit
Check gross margin on Screener.in over the last 5 to 10 years for a downward trend
Find A&P spend as a percentage of sales in the last three annual reports
Check whether the company's growth depends on discounts or festive promotions, from management commentary
Decide: is this a moat brand, or a famous name?

body.text: Brands and companies named are used to illustrate concepts from public information and are not investment recommendations. The spending trap and IPO examples are hypothetical.

points: Brand awareness can be bought with advertising; brand-based pricing power cannot be bought quickly
HMT, Onida, Kingfisher Airlines, and Jet Airways were household names that still could not protect their profits
Kingfisher shows that a brand strong in one industry cannot override the economics of another
Brands fail to protect profits when customers buy on price, technology shifts, the brand is stretched, fame depends on spending, or distribution changes
Rising A&P intensity with falling gross margins, even with flat market share, signals a brand that is rented, not owned
Judge a brand by stable margins and ROCE, not by recognition, followers, or advertising campaigns
